deviation_note: Source landed at 1313 words rather than the originally targeted 1700-2000. It was expanded once (added a fourth independent thread, on-call documentation cleanup, plus more detail in the checkout-service incident) and is left here rather than padded further, since additional padding risked diluting information density rather than adding genuine complexity. It is still substantially larger and more multi-threaded than the 'large' case (761 words, one buried root-cause chain, one set of near-identical siblings) — this case has four independent threads and two separate near-identical-sibling clusters (six checkout alerts, five connector fixes) plus the deliberately buried critical item.

questions.question: Which of the six checkout-service alerts this week actually mattered most, and why?
questions.gold_answer: The fourth alert (the payment-confirmation double-charge race condition) — it caused real financial harm to ~140 customers, remains unresolved in code, and was the only one missed by monitoring; the other five were routine and fully resolved.

questions.question: How many customers were double-charged, and over what time window?
questions.gold_answer: Approximately 140 customers, over a 40-minute window, roughly 09:10 to 09:50.

questions.question: Was the double-charge bug caught by automated monitoring, or discovered another way?
questions.gold_answer: Not caught by monitoring — it was discovered about six hours later via a customer support ticket.

questions.question: Has the fix for the double-charge race condition shipped yet?
questions.gold_answer: No — a design exists but hasn't been reviewed, and it's the single highest-priority unresolved item for checkout-service.

questions.question: Which mobile release depended on another release in the same train, and why?
questions.gold_answer: v3.14.3 depended on v3.14.1 — v3.14.1's null check was too aggressive and v3.14.3 had to narrow it.

questions.question: How many data-platform connectors broke from schema drift this week, and what did they have in common?
questions.gold_answer: Five connectors, all broken by the same class of failure — an upstream schema change (rename, addition, or drop) the connector's fixed mapping didn't account for.

questions.question: Why was the on-call runbook reorganized — because of a mishandled-alert incident, or something else?
questions.gold_answer: Something else — a new hire's difficulty finding the right section under time pressure; not any incident of the runbook causing a mishandled alert.

questions.question: Did the runbook reorganization change any actual alert-handling guidance?
questions.gold_answer: No — every surviving section's guidance is byte-for-byte the same; only the file layout and index changed.
